text: Lessons eleven and twelve gave you the AR, MA, ARMA, ARIMA, and SARIMA model families. This lesson is about choosing specific orders for a real series and then verifying the fitted model actually did its job, using the classical Box-Jenkins workflow.

Identify candidate orders from the shape of the ACF and PACF — a pure AR process has a PACF that cuts off sharply, while a pure MA process has an ACF that cuts off sharply instead. Then estimate a small grid of nearby candidates and compare them with AIC and BIC, where lower is better for both. Finally, diagnose: a correctly specified model should leave residuals that look like white noise, with no leftover autocorrelation.

A common pattern fits every small p, q combination in a loop, tracks each model's BIC, and keeps the order with the lowest value. BIC penalizes extra parameters more heavily than AIC does, so it tends to favor the simpler of two similarly fitting models.

To check residuals formally, run the Ljung-Box test on the fitted residuals at a chosen set of lags. Its null hypothesis is that there's no leftover autocorrelation. A small p-value, conventionally below 0.05, means that null is rejected — the residuals are not white noise, and the model needs more AR or MA terms before you trust its forecasts. A residual ACF plot and a simple plot of residuals over time are worth checking visually too.

Use ACF and PACF shape to suggest starting orders, AIC and BIC to compare nearby candidates, and the Ljung-Box test before trusting any fitted model. Next, lesson fourteen turns a diagnosed model into forecasts and shows how to evaluate them properly out of sample.
